children: By Kate King and Jim Carlton
SAN FRANCISCO-This city has a 1.5-million-square-foot hole in its AI-fueled renaissance: the downtown site of what was its biggest mall.

Not long ago, San Francisco Centre was a thriving retail destination, with a luxury day spa, nine-screen movie theater and department stores Nordstrom and Bloomingdale's drawing huge crowds. But the mall got sucked into a downward spiral during the pandemic. A surge in crime and homelessness followed.
The Market Street property closed earlier this year. A proposed sale collapsed in July.
Now, the mall is back on the market, with bids due Wednesday. Brokers expect it to sell for no more than $130 million-a shockingly meager sum compared with its $1.2 billion valuation a decade ago.
"It was such a trophy mall," said Vince Tibone, head of U.S. retail and industrial research at real-estate analytics firm Green Street. "It's had quite the demise."
Today, tall wooden boards topped with wire block off the San Francisco Centre's beaux-arts-style front entrance. The sidewalk is stained with urine.

The mall's struggles contrast sharply with most of the rest of the city, where investment in artificial intelligence is powering much of the comeback. The retail scene, housing market and office sector are flourishing. Job postings and venture-capital fundraising are way up. Rents in San Francisco are now back to the highest in the U.S.

Before Covid struck, San Francisco Centre was one of the top shopping destinations in the Bay Area. Annual sales of more than $1,000 a square foot put it in the top tier of mall-sales performance at a time when many other of these properties had fallen out of favor.
The mall was closed intermittently for seven months in 2020. When it reopened, shoplifting and homelessness kept the crowds away. They never returned.

In 2022, total sales at the mall were 35% below 2019 levels. Nordstrom delivered a critical blow in 2023 when it announced it would close, kicking off an exodus of retailers from the center, including Bloomingdale's. The mall's owner, Unibail-Rodamco-Westfield, said six weeks later it would stop making loan payments and turn the shopping center over to its lenders.
By last year, the nine-level complex looked more like a ghost town: 93% of its more than 1.5 million square feet were vacant. It was losing millions of dollars a year.

The mall's lenders, who were owed $558 million when the former owner walked away, reached a $130 million deal in March with two local firms to buy and redevelop the mall. But it fell through in July after the buyers decided the mall would be too complicated to redevelop.
San Francisco officials and retail analysts expect the mall will be repurposed into something else. Real-estate services firm CBRE is marketing the property for sale.

One potential bidder, local developer Urban Land Development, is exploring opening a multilevel sports complex in the former Nordstrom store that would include volleyball and soccer facilities as well as the basketball training program 94 Feet of Game, founded by NBA assistant coach and Bay Area native Phil Handy.

The previous deal fell through after the firms, Presidio Bay and Prado Group, spent months on due diligence and concluded the mall's complicated ownership structure and required approvals from city officials and others would make the urban mall too difficult to redevelop.

The former Bloomingdale's space, for example, is owned by the department store's parent company, Macy's Inc. Presidio Bay and Prado Group had reached a deal to purchase Bloomingdale's space, but further complications remained. A portion of the land underneath the mall is owned by the San Francisco Unified School District, which has been leasing it to the mall's owners.
"These mall redevelopments are so complex, requiring so many different parties to be on board," said Tibone, of Green Street.

Many of the streets surrounding San Francisco Centre are faring better. A new Ross Stores was bustling with customers on a recent afternoon. Apparel chain Uniqlo is returning with a new flagship after leaving the city five years ago. Mi Cocina, the kitchenware and outdoor-accessories retailer, left the mall and is reopening nearby this month.
"The market is healthy," said Alex Sagues, a senior vice president at CBRE. "Would it be better if the mall was open and operating? Yes, definitely."

Still, there are some positive signs for the mall's future. The school district has agreed to extend, through options, the property's ground lease through 2082, a move expected to reassure potential buyers.
And mall prices are up 13% over the past year, according to Green Street, as more investors become convinced that malls aren't as risky and ill-fated as previously feared.

But the clock is ticking for San Francisco Centre, which costs millions of dollars a year to maintain, even while closed, and will likely run out of cash within months, according to a person familiar with the matter.
